item.title: Mainstream Open Source Licenses: From MIT to AGPL, How Engineers Choose
item.description: In September 2017, React switched overnight from BSD+Patents to MIT. The reason: the Apache Software Foundation put React’s license on its “do not depend on” list, and Automattic (WordPress’s parent) immediately announced it would stop rewriting its UI on React. Facebook couldn’t withstand the ecosystem pressure and folded. Seven years later, in March 2024, Redis moved its core from BSD 3-Clause to a dual RSALv2+SSPL license — within a week AWS, Google, and Oracle jointly forked Valkey to replace it.

item.title: Shipping an App to Every NAS and Router OS: Packaging and Listing Differences Across fnOS, ZSpace, UGREEN, Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS, OpenWrt, and iStoreOS
item.description: In October 2024, TrueNAS SCALE 24.10 “Electric Eel” ripped out its k3s backend and moved the entire app layer from Helm Charts to Docker Compose. Overnight, every old tutorial telling you to add a “custom train” to TrueNAS stopped working — 24.10 also deleted the “Add Catalog” button. That same year, fnOS, ZSpace, and UGREEN each launched or rebuilt their app centers: fnOS’s .fpk, UGREEN’s freshly opened developer portal in May 2026, all racing to build an app ecosystem.

item.title: Operating System Selection by Scenario — OS Families, Workloads, and Engineering Trade-offs: Linux, Windows, and macOS
item.description:
About This Guide

This guide is organized not by OS version number, but by OS family and workload matching. The underlying dimensions of operating systems — OS family (Linux/Windows/macOS), kernel characteristics, package management, LTS support strategy, ecosystem fit — have been stable for years (Linux kernel evolution patterns are stable, the Windows NT kernel architecture is stable, macOS’s Unix foundation is stable), and hold more long-term reference value than specific version numbers.

item.title: A Map of Distributed Consensus: From Paxos to DAG-BFT — Boundaries and Selection Across Four Families
item.description: etcd uses Raft, Cosmos uses Tendermint, Bitcoin uses PoW, Sui uses Mysticeti — they’re all “consensus,” but they do not solve the same problem. Electing a leader among a few known nodes in a datacenter and reaching agreement on a ledger among anonymous nodes on a public chain sit a full order of magnitude apart in their assumptions. Mashing every consensus algorithm onto one throughput axis is why so many selection guides read like mush.

item.title: Motion Detection & Face Recognition on Edge Devices: The Resource–Accuracy Trade-off, from Classical to Lightweight AI
item.description: On a Raspberry Pi, an IPC SoC, or an AI box with only a fraction of a TOPS, the hard part of motion detection and face recognition isn’t whether you can do it — it’s how much resource you spend for how much accuracy. Once the compute and memory budget is fixed, every choice answers the same question: what can this tier solve, what can’t it, and what does it cost to close the gap.

item.title: The Edge AI Inflection: New Approaches to Motion Detection and Face Recognition Once NPUs Became Standard
item.description:
This is the sequel to “Motion Detection & Face Recognition: The Resource–Accuracy Trade-off.” That post’s central tension was compute scarcity — spend it carefully with frame differencing and ViBe, sprinkle in lightweight AI only when needed. This post tells the opposite story: once NPUs/TPUs move from optional to standard and compute stops being scarce, how does the playbook change.

The shift is real: a few years ago an edge IPC had only a CPU and you hoarded every cycle with background subtraction; now even cheap IPC SoCs ship a 6-TOPS NPU (Rockchip RK3588), Hailo-8 gives you 26 TOPS for 2.5W, and the Jetson Orin Nano Super — a firmware unlock on the same silicon — pushes sparse compute to 67 TOPS at $249. Detection is cheap enough to “always run,” so the two-tier “classical ROI gate, then AI” pipeline from the previous post begins to invert.
